turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Afternoon, Mr Dlamini, come sit. Your daughter phoned and said you're not yourself. What's been the main trouble?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm tired, doctor. That's the whole story. My legs are thick and I just want to sit.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been like this a while. The swelling in the ankles is back, and he's short of breath even walking to the loo. About two weeks.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): It's not two weeks. A few days. And it's not so much the walking — it's when I lie down, I have to sit up on the pillows. Don't speak for me.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, so I'm pinning it at somewhere between a few days and two weeks, worse when you lie flat. Any chest pain with that breathlessness?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): The chemist on Main Road was closed on Sunday. Gate down for load shedding. We stood in the parking like a pair of fools.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ja, that's a pain. I'm still on the chest, though. Any tightness or pain in the chest?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I'm not dying, if that's what you're after. I'm just finished.
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He isn't sleeping either. Up and down all night, kitchen light on, pacing about.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): I sleep fine. Leave it. I'm tired in the day because I'm old, not because I'm marching around at night.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll note that the two of you don't agree about the nights. The daytime tiredness — you feel that yourself?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. Washed out. Heavy in the bones. And these ankles.
[SEG0013] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He gets scratchy with me, shame, but that's not new. Sorry, Dad.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm sitting right here, Lindi. Talk to the man, not about me.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let's park the mood and look at the pills, because I suspect the box is mixed up in this. Who packs it?
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I do. I stay with him, I moved in after my mother passed, and I fill the weekly box every Sunday night.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Walk me through it, even if you only know them by colour. Start with the morning.

[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Morning is the water tablet, the furosemide. And the blood pressure one, enalapril, five milligrams... no, sorry, the packet says ten, ten milligrams. And another little white one I also put in the morning, which I thought was for the heart.
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): She counts that one twice. I told her. It's the same blooming water tablet from the hospital packet.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Let me think this out loud. The water tablet may be in the box twice. On the sister's note from this morning the repeat script says furosemide twenty milligrams.
[SEG0021] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, that's not right. The bottle from the chemist says forty milligrams, one in the morning. I've been giving the forty. I don't know where she got twenty.
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): And some days she drops in that extra white one from the hospital sleeve. Same tablet. I can see that much.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm not a hundred percent sure I put both in every day. If both were in the cupboard, some mornings both went in the box. I might have been doubling it.

[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): So the sister has written twenty, the bottle says forty, and there may be a second furosemide on top. I can't honestly write one dose for what you've actually been swallowing. We'll make a clean plan before you go.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): At night there's another tablet. A little white one. I don't know the name, and it's not the water tablet. He's had that one for years.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any letters on it, or a shape I might recognise?
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Round, plain, no writing I can see. He just calls it the little white one.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Don't look at me. I swallow what she hands me. I couldn't tell you one from the other.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Then I won't guess and get it wrong. That night one stays unnamed until I see the box. Is there a cholesterol tablet you do know?

[SEG0030] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Simvastatin, twenty milligrams at night. That's the bigger one, not the plain little white one. I nearly lumped them together just now, but they're separate, and I still don't know the little one's name.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Was anything stopped recently, by another doctor?

[SEG0032] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The amlodipine. The doctor at the provincial hospital stopped it, five milligrams. He reckoned the ankles were from that. It was a month ago... no, three weeks, three weeks back.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): He stopped it and the ankles are still fat. So what was the point.

[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Amlodipine can puff the ankles, but if they're still up three weeks later I'm thinking less about that tablet and more about the heart and how much water tablet you're on. You've still got the high blood pressure and the heart failure, ja?
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja. The pressure, for years. And they said the heart doesn't pump properly. You've got the file.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm only checking we're talking about the same problems. Any operations I should know about?
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): The bakkie's brakes are finished. That's the worry. I can't even get to the hardware.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No operations, doctor. He answered you about the bakkie. He's never been operated on.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Right, no surgery. I'll leave the bakkie alone. Do you smoke, or take a drink?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't smoke. Stopped when I was fifty. A beer on a Saturday, sometimes. That's all.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The smoking part is true. The beer is more than sometimes, a few beers most weekends. Not every night, though.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Former smoker, then, and a few beers at the weekends. Any heart attacks or strokes in the family?
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): My father had a stroke. He was old. I can't tell you the year, so don't ask.

[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): We can leave the year. Sister checked the pressure before you came in and wrote one hundred and fifty-eight over ninety-two. I counted the pulse at seventy-six... no, I lost one, it's eighty-four, and the finger probe is ninety-five percent.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Is ninety-five bad? Say it straight. I'm too tired for a long story.

[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ninety-five on room air is acceptable, not a crisis. One-fifty-eight over ninety-two is higher than I'd like, but I'm not changing three medicines today. Legs out, please.
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's been hiding the swelling in thick socks. The right one is worse, I think.

[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): Both sides pit when I press, the right a little more, up onto the shins. Chest is clear, I don't hear crackles. Heart sounds are regular, no murmur, and you're not in distress sitting there.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): The right shoe doesn't go on. I told her yesterday. Can I put my foot down?

[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ja, down you go. Thinking it through, there's known heart failure, swollen legs, breathlessness lying flat, and very likely too much furosemide. My working impression is the heart failure is flaring, with the extra water tablet adding to this washed-out feeling. Not a final label, just where I'm leaning.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): So the tablet you people gave me is the problem. Typical.

[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not exactly — the water tablet is still needed, it's the dose that's messy. I'm changing it to furosemide forty milligrams by mouth, once every morning. The extra one from the hospital packet comes out of the box and stays out.
[SEG0053] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): So forty, not the twenty the sister wrote, and not two of them. Just the one forty in the morning.

[SEG0054] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's the plan, and I'll write the script that way. Keep the enalapril at ten milligrams in the morning, and the simvastatin twenty at night. The nameless little white one, keep giving it for now, but bring the box so I can see what it really is.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): More instructions. My head is full already.

[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): One change only today, the water tablet, nothing else new. I do want bloods for urea and electrolytes, because too much furosemide plus the enalapril can knock the kidneys and the potassium. Sister can take it before you leave, or the lab this afternoon if the queue is mad.
[SEG0057] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll try before we go, if they're still open. Last time we came back and they'd shut the hatch.
[SEG0058] person_1 (DOCTOR): Ask at the desk on the way out. If the swelling hasn't settled when I see you again, we might book an echo of the heart. I'm not ordering that today.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): An echo. More driving. The bakkie has no brakes, Lindi, did you even tell him?
[SEG0060] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We'll take my car, Dad. It's sorted.

[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): If you get proper chest pain, or the breathing gets much worse, or you can't lie down at all, don't wait for me. Go to casualty. That's the safety bit, and then I'm done lecturing.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Ja, ja. Casualty. I heard you the first time.
[SEG0063] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Should I throw the hospital packet away, or just leave it out of the box?

[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): Leave it out and bring it with the other bottles next time, so we can read the label together. Don't bin it before I've seen it. Only one water tablet each morning from tonight... no, from tomorrow morning, you've had today's already.
[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Tomorrow morning. One. I can hold one thing in my head.
[SEG0066] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back in two weeks with the box. We'll look at the bloods and the ankles then.
[SEG0067] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Two weeks, I'll book it at reception. What if the blood result is ugly before that?
[SEG0068] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the lab phones with a bad result they'll tell you to come sooner, and if you're worried you can phone the rooms. Otherwise the two weeks stands.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): Are we finished? I need the toilet, and I need to sit in the car.
[SEG0070] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Nearly, Dad. Doctor, he hasn't been skipping the enalapril. It's only the water tablet I got muddled on.

[SEG0071] person_1 (DOCTOR): That helps, so the enalapril stays as it is. I'm still not sure how often the furosemide was doubled, and I'm not sure what that little white night tablet is. Those two wait for the box and the bloods. Anything else you wanted raised?
[SEG0072] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Just the legs and the tiredness. And tell that sister her twenty milligrams is nonsense.
[SEG0073] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heard. One forty-milligram water tablet in the morning, bloods today if they'll have you, the box next time, and two weeks. Off you go.

spec.situation: Older patient with a live-in carer or daughter who manages the pill box; names of tablets are described ('the little white one', 'the water tablet'), one was stopped by another doctor, one is double-counted. Doctor reviews and changes one medicine.
features: disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.

bad.reason: Daughter moved in after mother passed and fills pill box; transcript does not explicitly say wife died.

bad.reason: Morning furosemide is reported, but current use/frequency is uncertain due possible doubling.

omissions.text: Orthopnoea was specifically described: when he lies down he has to sit up on pillows; this key detail of the breathlessness was said by the patient.
The patient denied current smoking and said he has a beer on a Saturday, sometimes; the recorded alcohol history omits the patient's own account and only keeps the family member's higher estimate.
The doctor said not to change three medicines today because the oxygen saturation of 95% on room air was acceptable and not a crisis; the room-air context for oxygen saturation was stated.
The doctor instructed to keep the enalapril at 10 mg in the morning and the simvastatin 20 mg at night unchanged; this was an explicit medication plan, not just current use.
The doctor said the unnamed little white night tablet should be continued for now pending review of the box.
Bloods were to be done before leaving if possible, or at the lab that afternoon if the queue was too long; the timing/location detail of the urea and electrolytes plan was stated.
The follow-up purpose was stated: return in two weeks with the pill box so the doctor can review the blood results and ankle swelling.
